name: Iau
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand sources agree (2 agree, 0 refine), none contradicts

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant, rule 01 = second/final syllable of disyllables; stress non-lexical, tone carries the contrasts) rests on Bateman 1990 sec. 3.1 p.34, which I downloaded from sealang and confirmed verbatim on the page image, with the two illustrating forms on p.35 and the word-shape census on p.38 (c. 100 disyllabic nouns in a 3000-word dictionary, rest monosyllabic). This is the primary and only published phonology of Iau, by its principal describer; Glottolog lists no reference grammar, and the other phonology item (Edmondson et al. 1992, downloaded, pp. 92-98) is an instrumental tone study silent on stress. Clouse 1997 (downloaded) independently states stress is non-contrastive across Lakes Plain. Nothing found suggests a different coding. The record previously held no file and has an empty grade; the source is now obtained by the project with scanned and page images, so the strength of the evidence can b

sources.citation: Bateman 1990, Iau segmental and tone phonology, NUSA 32, sec.3.1 p.34, sealang.net scan read visually; only mono- and disyllables attested, 8 contrastive tones carry lexical/aspectual contrast, stress itself non-lexical
sources.quote: Stress in Iau is predictable. In disyllabic words, stress falls on the second syllable as illustrated below.

sources.citation: Bateman, Janet. 1990. Iau segmental and tone phonology. NUSA 32: 29-42.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'Stress in Iau is predictable. In disyllabic words, stress falls on the second syllable as illustrated below.' /sa3di3/ [sa3'di3] 'tree kangaroo', /da3dU2/ [da3'dU2] 'and'. p.38: ~3000-word dictionary has 'a little over one hundred nouns with two syllables. The other nouns are monosyllabic.'
sources.locator: sec. 3.1 p.34 (PDF p.6), examples top of p.35; sec. 4.4 p.38 on word shapes

sources.citation: Clouse, Duane A. 1997. Towards a reconstruction and reclassification of the Lakes Plain languages of Irian Jaya. In K. Franklin (ed.), Papers in Papuan linguistics No. 2, 133-236. Pacific Linguistics A-85.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date.' On Iau: 'Iau (Bateman 1990b, Edmonson et al. 1992) claims eight contrastive tones ... of the eight tones in Iau, four are short ... and the other four are nearly twice as long and occur on long (perhaps geminate?) vowels.'
sources.locator: sec. 11 'Tone typology' p.152; word-list conventions ( line 1329)

sources.quote: None. Instrumental F0 tracks of the 8 tones and tone clusters on monosyllables and of aspect tones; confirms Bateman's tone values ('results of this instrumental analysis confirm strongly the tone values assigned by Bateman (1991b)', p.96). No mention of stress in the pages available (99-103 missing from the publisher PDF).
sources.note: Held copy lacks the last five pages; low odds but the conclusion could comment on duration/intensity correlates relevant to the 'predictable stress' claim.
